title: From Jobs to Skills: Rethinking Vietnam’s FDI success
gist: Vietnam pulled in $34.65 billion of registered FDI in H1 2026, up 61 percent year-on-year, with realized FDI of $13.03 billion at a five-year first-half high — yet the wage premium for schooling, especially for university graduates, has been falling since the late 2000s, suggesting the economy is not generating enough skill-intensive jobs.

insights.claim: Vietnam attracted $34.65 billion in registered foreign direct investment in the first half of 2026, 61 percent more than the same period in 2025.
insights.speaker: Thi Hang Banh
insights.so_what: A 61 percent jump in registered FDI is a strong forward indicator for Vietnamese industrial property, construction, and power demand.

insights.claim: Vietnam's realized FDI reached $13.03 billion in H1 2026, its highest first-half level in five years, confirming that capital is actually being deployed rather than merely pledged.

insights.so_what: Realized-versus-registered gap matters: rising disbursement validates the near-term capex cycle rather than a registration-only headline.

insights.so_what: Export complexity is the standard bull case for Vietnam — the article sets it up as the consensus view it is about to complicate.

insights.claim: Vietnam's wage premium for staying in school has been falling since the late 2000s, with particularly marked declines for university graduates — a labor-market signal moving opposite to the headline FDI success.
insights.speaker: Thi Hang Banh
insights.so_what: A shrinking education premium undercuts the middle-class consumption story that usually accompanies an FDI boom.

insights.claim: The falling education premium likely reflects insufficient creation of jobs that make productive use of advanced skills, rather than any decline in the intrinsic value of education itself.
